title: Precision cascade strategy & KV coalescing — on-prem benchmarking

Clearview: run internal mixed-workload pass with provided prompt-set and share failures
action_items: Lena Hu: upload per-layer sensitivity heatmap and AWQ vs GPTQ scripts (due 2026-05-28)
Samir Patel: provide pricing delta for dedicated reserved capacity vs on-prem support (due 2026-05-25)

transcript:
[00:00:00] Meeting header: 2026-05-21 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~58m | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Hu (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Clearview CTO), Arjun Singh (ML Eng), Priya Rao (Infra)

Summary: quick on-prem benchmark recap, discuss a precision-cascade (FP8 -> INT8 -> AWQ/GPTQ fallback) strategy, KV coalescing/windowing to reduce small-request overhead, and next steps for pilot. Some audio drops, occasional mis-heard acronyms.

[00:00:15] Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have an hour on the calendar, i'll let lena drive the deep technical bits; quick intro — samir redwood ae — lena is our inference se. maya? you wanna kick off with your goals?

[00:00:32] Maya (Clearview): yeah thanks uh, so main thing for us is we need sub-150ms p95 for our chat assistant at 512 tokens across peak times, and cost needs to be comparable to our current GPU infra. also must keep all data inside our colo, so on-prem only.

[00:00:47] Lena (Redwood SE): got it; so constraints: latency SLO p95 150ms at 512, colocation (no cloud egress), and accuracy drop tolerances: less than 1.5% delta on our eval metric (intent-match). is that accurate?

[00:00:58] Maya: yeah that's the ballpark. we ran some early int8 runs and saw weird hallucinations on some prompts.

[00:01:06] Samir: perfect — that's why today's interesting. we'll walk through a precision cascade approach: start with FP8 in normal traffic, use layer-wise checks and fall back to AWQ/GPTQ/INT8 mixtures when we detect regression, plus KV coalescing to reduce small request overhead.

[00:01:22] Arjun (Clearview): small request overhead — can you clarify? our workload is 65% short prompts (<=64 tokens), 35% long (>=256).

[00:01:30] Lena: sure. short prompts cause a lot of per-request setup: kernel kickoff, small batch inefficiency, and kv cache churn. KV coalescing means we keep sticky KV entries for recent sessions and coalesce multiple short requests in a tiny window to amortize kernel launch cost. it's like micro-batching but with sticky kv affinity so latency doesn't climb much.

[00:01:52] Priya (Clearview): we worry about memory pressure — sticky KV increases RAM/GPU memory. how do you bound it?

[00:02:00] Lena: good point. two knobs: per-session KV TTL and max sticky sessions per worker. we observed at our lab runs that a 60s TTL with max 1k sticky sessions per GPU kept memory within 8GB overhead on A10-like cards for 7B models. but for larger models or FP8, numbers change.

[00:02:19] Maya: when you say FP8, are you using simulated FP8 or native hw FP8?

[00:02:25] Lena: currently simulated; most of our runtime kernels do block-fp8 emulation on FP16 SMs. full native fp8 on newer hw is route but not default. tradeoffs: FP8 tends to preserve more numeric range than naive int8 on some layers, but is more sensitive in layernorm and embedding layers.

[00:02:44] Arjun: and AWQ vs GPTQ? we tried GPTQ once — big accuracy hits on our fine-tuned models.

[00:02:51] Lena: yes. short summary: GPTQ is aggressive per-layer quantization with per-channel scales; tends to give smaller model size and good latency, but with some regression risk especially on fine-tuned heads. AWQ is more conservative, often per-tensor with additive compensation, less aggressive but safer. we recommend AWQ as first-pass for regulated workloads, and GPTQ for experimental cost-sensitive paths with strong eval harnesses.

[00:03:12] [00:03:18] Samir: want to show the lab bench numbers? lena, do you have the CSV?

[00:03:22] Lena: yeah i'll screen-share the run summary (link: https://redwood.internal/bench/onprem-demo-2026-05). quick tl;dr from our 7B tests on local 4xA100-sxm: FP16 baseline p95 @512 = 120ms; FP8 (sim) p95 = 110ms; INT8 (gptq) p95 = 95ms but with 2.8% intent-match drop on your prompt-set; AWQ p95 = 100ms with 0.8% drop.

[00:03:55] Maya: that's similar to our early numbers; the 2.8% on GPTQ is too high.

[00:04:00] Lena: right, so the idea is: cascade — prefer FP8/AWQ in steady state, flag inputs that are sensitive (we use a small regression classifier + data-driven delta), and escalate to full FP16 or alternative quantized fallback only when the classifier triggers. we maintain model variants locally so fallback cost is just routing and possibly warming kv.

[00:04:23] Arjun: how do you detect sensitivity online without causing too many fallbacks (which hurts cost)?

[00:04:28] Lena: two-level check: 1) fast prefix-score: run a compact comparator model (tiny 10-20M scoring head) against the prompt+topk to predict delta risk; 2) cheap canonical rerun sample for a subset of requests to calibrate drift. we tune the classifier threshold to hit target false-positive rate, e.g., 2% extra fallbacks overall.

[00:04:49] Priya: classifier adds compute too — what's that overhead?

[00:04:52] Lena: it's small — <2ms on CPU for most inputs if we keep it quantized and run as a microservice. The cost is worth it vs fallback to FP16 which is tens of ms.

[00:04:59] [00:05:10] Maya: all right, about KV coalescing windows — you mentioned 10ms vs 30ms earlier, how does that impact end-to-end latency?

[00:05:18] Lena: we ran microbenchmarks: short prompt p95 baseline no coalescing = 90ms (lots of single-shot inefficiency). 10ms coalescing window reduces p95 to 75ms but increases tail variance; 30ms reduces p95 to 60ms and improves GPU utilization by ~22% but increases tail for the very first token by ~12ms. so it's a tradeoff: bigger window is better for throughput but can hurt first-byte latencies for interactive users.

[00:05:45] Arjun: can we do adaptive windows per route? our chat UI has a 'fast' channel and a 'batch' channel.

[00:05:50] Samir: yes — routing policies are configurable per-route in Redwood: low-latency route enforces max-coalesce 10ms and higher-cost; batched routes get 30-50ms. sticky-session affinity is also tunable.

[00:06:03] Maya: on the topic of regression detection: you mentioned synthetic prompt-set. can you explain how that set is built?

[00:06:10] Lena: we generate a stratified set from production logs: sample by intent, length, and sensitive features. we then augment with edge cases and adversarial prompts from customers and public evals. redwood's eval harness runs AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 and computes delta on multiple metrics (intent-match, BLEU-ish heuristics, hallucination score). all runs are stored; diffs produce a regression-candidate list flagged for manual triage.

[00:06:37] Maya: manual triage is expensive. is there an automated rollback plan?

[00:06:40] Lena: yes — canary deployment + automatic rollback: if canary shows >1% drop on eval set in an hour, rollout reverses to previous variant. for on-prem we provide the orchestration manifest and a small operator agent you can run to manage rollouts.

[00:06:54] Priya: network wise, we have multi-rack NUMA nodes; any issues with PCIe/GPU locality for KV cache warm-ups?

[00:07:00] Lena: locality matters: KV warm-up across NUMA can create stalls. our recommendation: co-locate worker processes with attached GPUs on same NUMA node, use local NVMe for prefetching KV segments, and pre-warm top-k embeddings on startup. we also recommend using RDMA between racks if you have remote KV tiers to avoid PCIe bouncing.

[00:07:19] Arjun: interesting — on our cluster we saw a 30ms jitter spike when a worker GC'd. how do you mitigate GC pauses?

[00:07:24] Lena: avoid JVM-heavy components in the hot path; our runtime keeps the critical path in C++ and Python client is non-blocking. for any process that must run GC, track and schedule during low traffic, and prefer real-time-safe allocators.

[00:07:34] Samir: circling back to quantized fallbacks — one more nuance: mixed-precision per-layer gating. we found that only ~12% of layers are sensitive in many LLMs; gating those to FP16 while keeping rest INT8 gives most of the accuracy with small perf cost. we supply a per-layer sensitivity map and tooling to generate a mixed-precision config.

[00:07:57] Maya: that's promising. can you share an example of a mixed-precision config?

[00:08:02] Lena: yes — example: layers 0-4 embed/ln -> FP16, layers 5-18 -> AWQ-int8-ish, last 6 layers -> FP16 for decode head. I'll upload the actual yaml (note: link to sample yaml in the shared folder).

[00:08:15] [00:08:30] Arjun: what about stochastic rounding? we read a paper that suggested stochastic rounding reduces quantization bias vs deterministic rounding.

[00:08:36] Lena: stochastic rounding helps but has variance in outputs; it can hide systematic bias but may increase nondeterminism which you might not want in regulated flows. we use deterministic with per-channel scales for production, reserve stochastic for analysis runs.

[00:08:49] Maya: any surprising regressions you saw with AWQ on fine-tuned heads?

[00:08:53] Lena: sometimes AWQ changes tokenization-sensitive probabilities causing short-answer hallucinations; it's rare but when it happens it correlates strongly with very skewed embedding distributions in first layers. that's when we gate the embedding layers to FP16.

[00:09:08] Samir: quick note about storage: AWQ and GPTQ artifacts are different sizes and loading characteristics. GPTQ tends to have more per-layer metadata which can slow cold start. AWQ artifacts are somewhat larger than pure int8 but load faster in our runtime.

[00:09:21] Priya: and cold start — if a fallback triggers to FP16 variant, do you incur big cold-start latency?

[00:09:27] Lena: depends. if the FP16 model is pre-warmed on some reserved capacity, fallback routing is cheap (few ms). if you need to spin a new worker, cold start can be tens of seconds. our recommendation: keep a small pool of hot FP16 workers for fast fallback if your SLOs require it.

[00:09:41] Arjun: can Redwood run canaries locally in our colocation and push metrics to your console? we can't send our request logs to cloud though.

[00:09:48] Samir: yes — private agent setup supports pushing only aggregated metrics and traces (no raw prompts) to Redwood Console or you can self-host the observability stack. for security we support SAML SSO + customer KMS and audit logs.

[00:10:00] Maya: on the observability piece, can the system attribute regressions to specific layers or configs?

[00:10:05] Lena: yes — we do per-layer delta logging: output diffs, token-level surprise, and a regression attribution engine that scores layers by how often their gating prevents regressions in the eval set. we then produce a suggested minimal layer-rollback config.

[00:10:20] [00:10:25] Samir: show of hands — is the team comfortable with AWQ-first, mixed-precision gating, and sticky KV with a 10-30ms coalescing plan?

[00:10:30] Maya: sounds like a plan, but need those heatmaps and runs to trust it.

[00:10:33] Arjun: yep — we need the scripts so we can reproduce exactly.

[00:10:36] Priya: and a doc about memory knobs — per-session kv ttl, max sticky sessions, nvme prefetch config.

[00:10:42] Lena: noted — i'll drop links after the call. artifacts: small-run CSVs, layer-sensitivity heatmaps, example mixed-precision yaml, coalescing perf logs (link: https://redwood.internal/bench/onprem-demo-2026-05/artifacts).

[00:10:56] [00:11:15] Technical Q&A rapid fire
[00:11:18] Arjun: What about dequant bias accumulating over long generations?

[00:11:22] Lena: we observed for chains >1024 tokens, small bias can accumulate, especially with int8-only. mitigation: periodic re-normalization layers in mixed precision or checkpointed partial recompute to FP16 for long contexts. also increasing kv precision for long-lived sessions helps.

[00:11:40] Maya: are there known interactions between coalescing and token streaming (we stream tokens to users)?

[00:11:45] Lena: yes — streaming plus coalescing needs careful design: you can emit tokens for the first request in a coalesced batch as soon as partial decode is available, but you must ensure KV affinity is preserved. we offer token-level plumbing in the runtime to avoid buffering the whole response.

[00:12:00] Arjun: any recommendation for per-route SLOs config?

[00:12:03] Samir: low-latency route: p95 target 150ms, coalesce 10ms, no sticky >200 sessions per GPU, reserve 10% hot FP16 for fallback. cost route: p95 250ms, coalesce 30-50ms, allow more sticky sessions.

[00:12:18] Priya: for our infra, what would be the recommended starting cluster size for a pilot?

[00:12:22] Lena: for 7B model and your traffic (~65% short), starting point: 4 GPUs per zone (A100/40960 or equivalent) with 2 hot FP16 workers and rest quantized; adjust after week-1 telemetry. exact numbers depend on concurrency — share your qps and we'll provide a calced estimate.

[00:12:41] Maya: we'll send qps histogram and token-length distributions.

[00:12:44] [00:12:50] Samir: i want to capture a couple of action items — lena will share heatmaps and YAML, i'll send pricing delta, arjun/priaya will run coalescing tests with 10/30ms windows. any other blockers?

[00:13:03] Arjun: one more — how does Redwood handle model artifact signing/verifying for on-prem? we need to ensure no tampering.

[00:13:08] Lena: artifacts are signed with customer KMS or our signing keys depending on deployment model; for private deployments you can manage keys entirely and use local verification. we provide a utility for signature verification at load time.

[00:13:20] Maya: good. also SOC2/ISO question — do you have references?

[00:13:23] Samir: yes — we have SOC2 Type II, ISO27001. i'll DM the cert links after the call.

[00:13:30] [00:13:35] Noise / brief audio glitch (some words missing)

[00:13:50] Lena: slightly shifting topic — regression hunting playbook: 1) run eval harness on pre-flight submissions; 2) run quick A/B on small canary traffic; 3) if regression found, run bisect on per-layer configs using our automated bisector to identify the minimal set of layers to un-quantize. the bisector typically needs ~20-40 eval runs.

[00:14:12] Arjun: how long are those eval runs?

[00:14:15] Lena: each eval run depends on prompt-set size; for our 5k prompt-set it's ~7 minutes with 4 workers; can be parallelized.

[00:14:22] Maya: any caveats about AWQ/GPTQ tool licensing?

[00:14:27] Samir: both are OSS variants; we include util wrappers. for any third-party libs with different licenses we'll flag them in the artifact.

[00:14:33] Priya: what about determinism — for audit we need reproducible results across runs. quantization can introduce nondeterminism — is that a blocker?

[00:14:39] Lena: we can run with deterministic kernels and fixed seeds for the quant steps; GPTQ training may include small nondet steps but for inference we can make reproducible quant artifacts. we'll document seeding steps.

[00:14:56] [00:15:10] Live debugging vignette (speaker overlap, some crosstalk)

[00:15:30] Arjun: if we see a 1.2% delta on intent-match, is that acceptable? our threshold is 1.5% but we want to avoid regression accumulation.

[00:15:36] Maya: i'd prefer 1% but 1.5% is our hard stop.

[00:15:40] Samir: ok — we'll tune the cascade to aim for <1% FP8/AWQ drift and keep GPTQ limited to <0.5% of traffic as an opt-in experimental lane.

[00:15:51] Lena: note on evaluation: measure both global metric and per-intent delta; small global deltas can hide large intent-specific regressions.

[00:15:59] [00:16:10] Discussion of bench artifacts and logs format (parquet/CSV), agreed on CSV + gz for initial share.

[00:16:22] Arjun: will you share the layer-sensitivity heatmap as both CSV and PNG?

[00:16:26] Lena: yes — csv + png + the script to regenerate.

[00:16:30] Maya: timeline — can we aim to start pilot in two weeks?

[00:16:34] Samir: target week of 2026-06-08, ok?

[00:16:37] Maya: yes.

[00:16:40] [00:16:45] Closing recap by Samir: share artifacts, run coalescing tests, schedule pilot kickoff; flag any security docs.

[00:16:55] Some small talk, latencies, and sign-off.

[00:17:05] End of recorded transcript (store truncated if needed).

Note: Transcript contains occasional mis-hears — e.g., "gptq" sometimes transcribed as "g p t q" or "gpt q"; "KV" occasionally becomes "K V". Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.internal/bench/onprem-demo-2026-05 (CSV logs), sample-mixed-precision.yaml, per-layer-heatmap.png.
